name: Philadelphia
title: Investor Renovation Contractor in Philadelphia, PA | Genstone
metaDescription: Rowhouse rehabs for Philadelphia investors: flips, BRRRR, rentals, duplexes, 203(k) and REO, scoped by block with L&I permits and draws tied to finished work.
intro: Philadelphia is a rowhouse city, and that single fact shapes nearly every renovation budget an investor writes here. Most of the houses you will buy share at least one party wall, sit on a fieldstone or brick foundation that has been taking on water for a century, and carry a flat roof last coated by someone the seller cannot name. Genstone Construction renovates these properties for investors, lenders and servicers by coordinating vetted, licensed local contractors in Philadelphia, with a designated field manager on your project and oversight from our Romeoville, Illinois headquarters. Before you commit capital, our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates repairs and pressure-tests the after-repair value against the specific block, because two rowhouses a few doors apart in Point Breeze or Kensington can support very different finish levels. From there you get a written scope with labor, materials and a draw schedule, permits pulled through the Department of Licenses and Inspections, lien waivers collected, and progress you can follow without crossing the Schuylkill to check on it.
housingStock:
The oldest investor-grade stock in Philadelphia is the two-story brick workers' rowhouse of the mid and late 1800s, packed onto narrow lots in Kensington, Fishtown, Port Richmond, Point Breeze and much of South Philadelphia. Many have a single front room, a kitchen in a rear ell, a tight winding or straight-run stair, and a basement with a dirt or thin concrete floor over rubble stone. North of Girard and in Brewerytown, Strawberry Mansion and Francisville you also find taller three-story Victorian rowhouses with deep lots, bay fronts and ornate cornices, many of which were split into apartments decades ago.

West Philadelphia and Germantown add a different layer: large stone and brick twins from the late 1800s and early 1900s, often with slate or tile roofs, wraparound porches and boiler-fed radiators. Through Olney, Logan, Cobbs Creek, Kingsessing and Wynnefield, the 1910s and 1920s produced porch-front rowhouses with front lawns and finished-height basements. After the Second World War, the Northeast filled in with brick rowhomes that have built-in garages and rear driveways in Mayfair, Oxford Circle and Rhawnhurst, alongside two-story stacked duplexes with one apartment per floor.

What ties nearly all of it together is masonry. Floor joists usually span side to side and bear in pockets cut into the party walls, which means interior partitions are often non-bearing and open plans are easier than buyers expect. It also means the party walls, the front and rear facades and the roof flashing are the structure, so repointing with a compatible soft mortar, checking joist ends for rot, and tying bowed walls back in are core rehab tasks rather than extras. Expect plaster on lath, layers of pre-1978 lead paint, ungrounded or knob-and-tube wiring in older blocks, galvanized supply piping, and cast-iron or terra cotta drains that run under the basement floor to the street.

commonIssues.title: Flat roofs and party-wall flashing
commonIssues.body: Most rowhouse roofs in Philadelphia are low-slope membranes that tie into the neighbor's roof at the party wall. Leaks often start at that seam, at the parapet coping, or where a chimney was abandoned and patched. Recoating over a failing membrane only buys a season. Our scope usually calls for tearing off to the deck, replacing rotted sheathing, installing a new membrane with proper termination at both party walls, and correcting the slope toward the scupper or rear gutter so water stops ponding over the back bedroom.

commonIssues.title: Wet basements and owner-owned sewer laterals
commonIssues.body: Rubble-stone basement walls take on water through decayed mortar, and many houses still drain through original terra cotta or cast-iron laterals. The Philadelphia Water Department treats the lateral as the owner's responsibility, so a collapsed line under the sidewalk or street becomes your repair. We recommend a camera inspection on nearly every pre-war purchase, then budget for parging or repointing the walls, regrading the rear yard or areaway, and lining or replacing the lateral where the footage shows root intrusion or sags.

commonIssues.title: Bowed walls and tired joist pockets
commonIssues.body: Rear walls on older rowhouses tend to bow outward when roof water has been running down the masonry for years. Joist ends that sit in damp pockets lose bearing, and the floor above starts to slope toward the back of the house. The fix ranges from star-bolt tie rods and repointing to rebuilding a section of wall and sistering joists. Catching this before you price a flip matters, because it is a structural item that requires an L&I permit and changes the schedule.

commonIssues.title: Lead paint and rental certification
commonIssues.body: Nearly every Philadelphia rowhouse an investor buys predates 1978, and most have original lead-based paint under later coats, especially on windows, door jambs and porch trim. That affects work practices during demolition and sanding, and for rentals it ties into the city's requirement that landlords of older units certify them as lead-safe or lead-free before leasing. We plan window replacement, friction-surface treatment and specialized cleaning into rental scopes so the dust-wipe clearance test passes the first time.

commonIssues.title: Outdated electrical and old supply lines
commonIssues.body: Fuse panels, ungrounded two-wire circuits and pockets of knob-and-tube wiring are still common, particularly in Kensington, Port Richmond and South Philadelphia. Galvanized supply piping corrodes from the inside, restricts flow to second-floor baths and often connects to an aging service line. Rewiring a rowhouse is easier with walls open, so we tie electrical and plumbing replacement to the demolition phase. Insurers and lenders frequently ask about panel type and wiring, which makes this a financing issue as much as a safety one.

investorMarket:
Philadelphia works for several strategies at once because its neighborhoods sit at very different points in their price cycles. Flips tend to make the most sense where new-construction townhomes have already reset buyer expectations nearby, such as the edges of Fishtown, East Kensington, Point Breeze, Brewerytown and the blocks around East Passyunk. There, a well-finished rehab of an older rowhouse can compete on price with new builds while offering original brick and detail.

Buy-and-hold investors gravitate toward the Northeast, Olney, Frankford, Kingsessing, Cobbs Creek and parts of Germantown, where porch-front and post-war rowhomes rent steadily and purchase prices leave room for a full systems update. BRRRR works when the scope is heavy enough to move the appraisal but the house is still on a street where renovated rentals have closed recently, so the appraiser has evidence.

Small multifamily is concentrated in West Philadelphia, Germantown, Mount Airy and the larger Victorian rowhouses of North Philadelphia, where older conversions produced two, three and four units in one building. Those deals hinge on confirming the legal unit count before closing. Bank-owned and servicer inventory appears across North, Southwest and lower Northeast Philadelphia, often with code violations and vacant-property obligations already attached. In every case, the block matters more than the zip code, and our Pre-Offer Rehab Review is built to price the house you are actually buying, not a neighborhood average.
permits:
Building, electrical, plumbing, mechanical and zoning permits in Philadelphia are issued by the Department of Licenses and Inspections, which runs applications through its eCLIPSE online system. Structural work such as rebuilding a rear wall, cutting new openings in masonry, replacing joists or adding a roof deck needs a building permit with drawings, and roof decks frequently need zoning review as well. Electrical and plumbing work must be performed and permitted by trades licensed in the city, and any contractor working on a Philadelphia property needs a Philadelphia contractor license along with Pennsylvania home improvement registration.

Changing the number of units, adding a unit to a rowhouse or changing a use usually requires a zoning permit and may need a variance from the Zoning Board of Adjustment. Properties inside a local historic district or individually listed on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places need Philadelphia Historical Commission approval for exterior changes, including windows and cornices. Rentals need a rental license and a Certificate of Rental Suitability, and older rental units must meet the lead certification rules. Genstone's field manager tracks each application, schedules inspections and keeps the permit record with your project documents.
climate: Philadelphia sits where hot, humid summers meet cold, wet winters, and its masonry houses feel both. Freeze-thaw cycles work water into soft mortar joints, spall brick faces and lift front steps, which is why repointing and step repairs show up on so many scopes. Summer humidity drives condensation and mildew in basements that were never meant to be living space, so dehumidification and drainage need to be solved before anyone finishes a basement. Heavy rain events have flooded low-lying areas near the Schuylkill, including Manayunk and Eastwick, and street flooding can back sewage into basements without a working backwater valve. For scheduling, roofing and masonry are easiest from spring through early fall, while interior systems and finish work can run through winter once the building is weathertight and the heat is on.

faqs.q: Do you work in every Philadelphia neighborhood?
faqs.a: We coordinate vetted, licensed local contractors throughout the city, from South and West Philadelphia to Kensington, Germantown and the Northeast, and in close-in suburbs such as Upper Darby and Cheltenham. Genstone does not keep a local office in Philadelphia; projects are run from our Romeoville, Illinois headquarters with a designated field manager assigned to your job. That manager handles scheduling, permits with Licenses and Inspections, inspections and documentation, so you can follow progress without being on site.

faqs.q: How do you estimate a rowhouse before I make an offer?
faqs.a: Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review looks at the house you are bidding on, its roof, masonry, basement, systems and layout, then estimates repairs and checks the after-repair value against nearby sales on the same or similar blocks. In Philadelphia, that comparison has to be tight, because finish expectations and values can change within a few streets. If the numbers do not support your offer, you find that out before your deposit goes hard.

faqs.q: Is there a deposit before a Philadelphia rehab starts?
faqs.a: No. Genstone does not ask for upfront payment. Each draw follows a finished, photographed stage of the rowhouse work, and the last payment waits until the job is done and you have signed off. Dumpster and debris costs are built into the estimate, which matters in Philadelphia because rowhouse demolition often means hauling plaster and lath out through a single front door and arranging a dumpster or right-of-way permit on a narrow street.

faqs.q: Is there a warranty on the work?
faqs.a: Yes. Every Philadelphia job is backed by a one-year workmanship warranty. It covers defects in the work we performed, such as a roof membrane seam that was not sealed properly or a fixture that was installed incorrectly. It does not cover tenant damage or normal wear and tear, which is worth noting for rental owners whose properties see heavy use between turns. If something we installed fails within that year, your field manager arranges the correction.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Philadelphia, PA | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Philadelphia flip renovations priced block by block: rowhouse roofs, rear walls, open plans and basements, with L&I permits and draws tied to finished work.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Philadelphia
fix-flip.intro: Flipping in Philadelphia is a block-by-block game. A rehabbed rowhouse in East Kensington or Point Breeze may be competing with brand-new townhomes around the corner, while a similar house a few streets over sells to a buyer who mostly wants a dry basement and a modern kitchen. Genstone Construction helps you decide which buyer you are building for before you close. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates the repairs, checks the after-repair value against recent sales on comparable blocks, and flags the structural surprises common to Philadelphia rowhouses, like bowed rear walls and failing laterals, that can quietly eat a flip margin. Once you buy, a designated field manager coordinates vetted local contractors, pulls permits through Licenses and Inspections and keeps your draw schedule tied to finished work.

sections.h2: Matching the finish level to the block, not the zip code
sections.body:
In parts of Fishtown, Brewerytown and Point Breeze, the comps that matter are newer townhomes with roof decks, finished basements and full-width kitchens. If your flip sits in that pool, buyers will compare your rehab to new construction and expect open living space, a second full bath and outdoor space. A few blocks away, the comparable sales may be older rowhouses with updated kitchens and baths, and spending on a roof deck there simply raises your basis without moving the sale price.

Our estimators build multiple ARV plans for that reason. One plan might keep the existing layout and focus on systems, kitchen and bath. Another might add a second-floor bath, open the first floor and finish the basement. Each comes with its own scope, cost and projected value, so you can see which version the block supports. We also look closely at what new construction nearby is offering, because in Philadelphia the builder down the street often sets the bar for what a buyer expects to see in a listing.

sections.h2: Where rowhouse flip budgets actually go
sections.body:
Because joists in most Philadelphia rowhouses run between the party walls, many interior walls can come out without heavy beam work, which is why open first floors are so common in flips here. The money tends to go elsewhere. Rear walls and joist pockets are the first place we look, since a bowed back wall or rotted joist ends must be fixed before any finishes go in. Roofs are almost always replaced on a flip, with careful flashing at both party walls.

Basements are the other big decision. Buyers like a finished lower level, but many Philadelphia basements have low ceiling height, rubble walls and a sewer line running under the slab. Finishing one well means drainage, waterproofing, a backwater valve where needed and egress or ceiling height that passes inspection. Sometimes the smarter flip leaves the basement clean, dry and unfinished. Exposed brick walls are popular, but repointing old brick for display costs more than drywall, so we price it as a deliberate choice rather than a default.

sections.h2: Keeping carrying costs under control on a Philadelphia timeline
sections.body:
Every month a flip sits unfinished costs you interest, insurance and property taxes, so sequencing matters. Licenses and Inspections reviews structural and zoning applications before work can start on those items, and roof decks or unit changes can add zoning steps. We prepare permit packages early, often before closing when the seller allows access, so the clock on approvals starts sooner.

Once permits are in hand, the field manager sequences demolition, structural repair, rough-in for plumbing and electrical, inspections, and then insulation and drywall. Narrow streets add a practical constraint: dumpsters and material deliveries may need a right-of-way permit and careful timing on blocks with tight parking, and that cost is already inside our estimate. You see photos and milestone updates as each stage closes, and draws are released against completed work. When the house is finished, you receive the permit record, lien waivers and documentation that buyers' agents and inspectors tend to ask about.

faqs.q: Should I add a roof deck to my Philadelphia flip?
faqs.a: It depends on the comps. Where new-construction townhomes with decks are selling nearby, a deck can help a rehab compete. Elsewhere, buyers may not pay for it. A roof deck also needs a building permit, often zoning review, structural framing and careful roofing, so it is never a small add-on. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review can price your flip with and without a deck so you can decide on numbers rather than habit.

faqs.q: How do you handle a bowed rear wall found during demolition?
faqs.a: Your field manager documents it with photos, our estimator prices the repair, and you approve a change order before work proceeds. Typical solutions include tie rods with star plates, rebuilding the damaged section and sistering weakened joists. Because it is structural, it requires a permit from Licenses and Inspections. When we can see warning signs before you buy, such as cracking at window heads or sloping floors, we include them in the original estimate instead.

faqs.q: Can you renovate a flip while I am out of state?
faqs.a: Yes. Many of our Philadelphia clients never visit the property during construction. Your field manager coordinates local contractors, manages permits and inspections, and posts progress photos and milestone updates. Draws are released only for completed work, and final payment waits for completion and your approval. Genstone manages projects from our Romeoville, Illinois headquarters, and the trades on site are vetted, licensed local contractors.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Contractor in Philadelphia, PA | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: Philadelphia BRRRR rehabs built for the refinance appraisal and the rental license: durable rowhouse scopes, lead-safe work and draws tied to finished work.
brrrr.intro: A Philadelphia BRRRR deal lives or dies on two inspections that have nothing to do with each other: the appraiser who sets your refinance value and the city requirements that let you legally lease the house. Genstone Construction scopes for both. We help investors rehab porch-front rowhouses in Olney and Kingsessing, post-war rowhomes in Mayfair and the Northeast, and older brick houses in Frankford and Germantown so they appraise against renovated comparables and come out ready for a rental license, lead certification and a tenant. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates the work and checks whether the after-repair value supports your refinance before you buy. After closing, a designated field manager coordinates vetted local contractors, handles permits through Licenses and Inspections, and ties every draw to completed work.

sections.body:
An appraiser valuing a renovated Philadelphia rowhouse will look for nearby sales of similar houses in similar condition, usually on the same or adjacent blocks. If renovated rentals on your street have sold recently, a full systems and finish update can move the value meaningfully. If the only comps are unrenovated estate sales, even an excellent rehab may appraise below your target.

That is why our estimators study the comparable sales before recommending a scope. Appraisers notice the items that show up on a report: a new roof, updated electrical service, a modern kitchen, a renovated bath, replaced windows and a dry basement. They give less weight to decorative upgrades. In the Northeast, for example, a finished lower level with a garage that works can help a rowhome compare well. In older South or North Philadelphia blocks, a second bath can matter more. We document every improvement with photos and an itemized list so you can hand the lender and appraiser a clear record of what was done.

sections.h2: Getting the house legally rentable in Philadelphia
sections.body:
The refinance is only half the plan. Before a tenant moves in, a Philadelphia rental needs a rental license from Licenses and Inspections and a Certificate of Rental Suitability, and older units must be certified lead-safe or lead-free. Those requirements shape the scope from the start.

On pre-1978 houses, lead certification usually means addressing friction and impact surfaces such as old windows, door jambs and stair treads, stabilizing deteriorated paint, and finishing with specialized cleaning so the dust-wipe test passes. Working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, safe egress, handrails and functioning heat are basic expectations. If you plan to rent through the Philadelphia Housing Authority voucher program, the unit will also face that program's inspection, so we build its common failure points into the punch list: GFCI protection near water, secure railings, working windows and no peeling paint. Planning for these up front avoids a second mobilization after the refinance closes.

A BRRRR property has to hold up for years of tenants, so materials are chosen for durability and easy repair. Luxury vinyl plank stands up to wet boots and pet traffic better than refinished pine floors in most rental rooms. Semi-gloss paint in kitchens and baths cleans easily. Solid-surface or laminate counters are simple to replace.

Systems deserve the most attention. Many Philadelphia rowhouses heat with an older boiler and radiators, and replacing a working hydronic system with forced air is rarely worth it. Servicing or replacing the boiler and adding ductless units for cooling often makes more sense in houses without ductwork. We replace galvanized supply lines, bring panels up to modern service, and camera the sewer lateral, because a backup in the basement is one of the most expensive calls a landlord takes. The goal is a house that appraises well, rents quickly and stays quiet between turns.

faqs.q: What scope usually moves a Philadelphia rowhouse appraisal?
faqs.a: Items that appear clearly on an appraisal report tend to matter most: roof, electrical service, plumbing, heating, kitchen, bath, windows and a dry basement. A second bath can help in older rowhouse blocks where most comparables have only one. Decorative extras often add cost without value. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review compares your house with recent renovated sales nearby so the scope targets what the appraiser is likely to credit.

faqs.q: Can you prepare the property for a rental license and lead certification?
faqs.a: Yes. We plan the rehab so the house is ready for a Philadelphia rental license, a Certificate of Rental Suitability and lead certification on pre-1978 units. That includes lead-safe work practices, attention to windows and friction surfaces, and thorough final cleaning before dust-wipe testing. We also cover alarms, egress, railings and heat so the house is ready to lease when construction ends.

faqs.q: Does Genstone help with financing for BRRRR deals?
faqs.a: Within the Genstone Companies, Genstone Financial lends to investors through fix-and-flip loans, DSCR rental loans, lines of credit and new construction loans. Some investors use a fix-and-flip loan for the purchase and rehab, then refinance into a DSCR loan once the property is leased. Nothing requires you to borrow from a Genstone company, either. Our scope, draw schedule and documentation are built to work with lender draw processes either way.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Philadelphia | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Single-family rental rehabs across Philadelphia rowhouse neighborhoods: standard specs, durable finishes, lead-safe work and turns managed without site visits.
rental-renovation.intro: Owning rentals in Philadelphia usually means owning rowhouses from several eras at once: an 1890s brick house in Port Richmond, a 1920s porch-front in Olney, a post-war garage rowhome in Mayfair. Each ages differently, and a portfolio stays manageable only when the renovation standard is consistent across all of them. Genstone Construction renovates and turns single-family rentals for individual landlords, funds and REITs, coordinating vetted, licensed local contractors with a designated field manager on each job. We build a rental spec that fits Philadelphia housing, keep every unit lead-safe and ready for licensing, and document the work so you can manage a scattered portfolio without visiting every address. Draws are tied to completed work, and you can follow progress, photos and milestones online from anywhere.

sections.h2: One rental standard across very different rowhouses
sections.body:
Portfolio owners in Philadelphia often inherit a patchwork: one house with a new kitchen and an old roof, another with a fresh roof and a fuse panel. We start by writing a rental standard that applies across your properties, then adapt it to each house type.

The standard typically fixes the finish choices: one flooring product, one paint color family, one cabinet and countertop line, one fixture package. That simplifies future repairs and lets your maintenance team stock parts. The adaptation is where local knowledge matters. A pre-war rowhouse in Kensington may need repointing, a new membrane roof and lateral work before finishes make sense. A porch-front in Cobbs Creek often needs porch roof and column repair, which is a frequent source of leaks and code complaints. A Northeast rowhome may need garage door, driveway drainage and rear patio work. Each scope lists what the house needs to meet your standard, so you can compare costs across the portfolio instead of approving one-off quotes.

A rental turn here usually involves more than paint and cleaning. Older Philadelphia rowhouses see steady wear on stairs, railings and windows, and a turn is the right time to fix them before they become code items. Our turn scopes cover patching and painting, flooring repair or replacement, fixture and appliance checks, smoke and carbon monoxide alarm replacement, and a walk-through of the roof, basement and sewer cleanout for early signs of trouble.

Lead rules make the paint work more careful than in newer markets. On pre-1978 units, disturbing painted surfaces calls for lead-safe practices, and recertification may require new dust-wipe testing. We build that into the timeline so the unit is ready for the next lease without a failed clearance pushing back move-in. Genstone Field Services, part of the Genstone Companies, also handles turn and make-ready work, inspections and occupied maintenance, which helps owners who want one team responsible for both renovation and upkeep.

sections.h2: The systems that drive Philadelphia maintenance calls
sections.body:
Most expensive landlord calls in Philadelphia trace back to the same few systems. Flat roofs that were patched instead of replaced leak into the back bedroom. Terra cotta laterals clog with roots and back up into the basement. Galvanized supply lines lose pressure and start to pinhole. Old boilers fail on the coldest night of the year.

Renovation is the cheapest moment to deal with these because the walls and ceilings are already open. Our rental scopes routinely include roof replacement with proper party-wall flashing, a camera inspection and lining or replacement of the sewer lateral, new PEX or copper supply lines, a new panel with grounded circuits and a serviced or replaced boiler. Where houses lack ductwork, ductless cooling is often more practical than window units, which tenants tend to install poorly. Addressing these systems once lowers future emergency calls and gives you better documentation for insurance and lenders.

faqs.q: Can you renovate rentals spread across different Philadelphia neighborhoods?
faqs.a: Yes. Many of our Philadelphia clients own scattered rowhouses rather than a single block. We assign a field manager, apply one renovation standard across your properties and coordinate vetted local contractors for each address. You receive a separate scope, schedule and draw record for every house, with photos and milestones posted online, so you can track a portfolio from out of state.

faqs.q: How do you handle lead paint in older rental units?
faqs.a: We assume original lead paint is present in pre-1978 houses unless testing shows otherwise. Scopes include lead-safe work practices when painted surfaces are disturbed, attention to windows, doors and stairs, and specialized cleaning before dust-wipe clearance. That supports Philadelphia's lead certification requirement for rentals and reduces the chance of a failed test delaying a lease. Where an older unit has original wood windows, replacing them during the renovation often removes the largest single source of lead dust in the house.

faqs.q: Do you offer ongoing maintenance as well as renovation?
faqs.a: Genstone Field Services, part of the Genstone Companies, provides inspections, occupied maintenance, turn and make-ready work, property preservation and code compliance. Genstone Property Management is also part of the group. Owners can use those services alongside our renovation work or keep their own manager and maintenance providers. Either way, our documentation is organized so whoever manages the house can see what was done.

multifamily-renovation.title: Duplex and 2-4 Unit Renovation, Philadelphia | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Renovating Philadelphia duplexes and 2-4 unit conversions: Northeast stacked duplexes, West Philly twins, legal unit counts, fire separation and phasing.
multifamily-renovation.h1: Duplex and 2–4 Unit Renovations in Philadelphia
multifamily-renovation.intro: Philadelphia's small multifamily stock rarely looks like a purpose-built apartment building. It is a stacked duplex in Oxford Circle or Rhawnhurst, a West Philadelphia twin carved into three apartments decades ago, or a tall North Philadelphia rowhouse with a unit on each floor. These buildings can perform well, but they come with questions single-family rehabs never raise: how many units are legally permitted, whether the fire separation between them is real, and how to work around tenants who are staying. Genstone Construction renovates two- to four-unit properties in Philadelphia for investors, funds and lenders. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review checks the scope and value before you buy, and a designated field manager coordinates vetted local contractors, permits through Licenses and Inspections and phasing for occupied units.

sections.h2: Confirming the legal unit count before you buy
sections.body:
Many Philadelphia buildings have more kitchens than their zoning permits. A Victorian twin in Spruce Hill or Germantown may have been converted to three apartments generations ago with no record, or a rowhouse may have gained a basement unit without approval. The legal count matters because it affects value, financing, the rental license and what Licenses and Inspections will let you permit.

Before closing, we recommend checking the zoning permit history and certificate of occupancy for the property. If the legal count is lower than the current layout, you can price the deal as it is legally allowed, or plan to seek approval for the additional unit, which may require a zoning permit and possibly a variance from the Zoning Board of Adjustment. Our estimators can scope both paths, including the extra fire separation, egress and separate utilities a legalized unit would need, so you know the cost of each before committing capital.

sections.h2: Shared systems and fire separation in older conversions
sections.body:
Older conversions often share more than a wall. It is common to find one boiler heating several apartments, a single water heater, one electric service split with subpanels, and a common stair that doubles as the only exit for the upper unit. In Northeast stacked duplexes, the layout is cleaner, but the separation between floors and shared basements still needs attention.

Renovation is the moment to decide how much to separate. Individual electric meters and panels let tenants pay their own power and reduce disputes. Separate heating systems cost more upfront but simplify billing and maintenance. Fire separation between units, rated doors at unit entrances, interconnected smoke alarms and safe egress are code issues, not upgrades, and they are frequently missing in informal conversions. We scope each building based on what is there and what the code requires for its legal use, so your rehab passes inspection and the building is safer for the people who live in it.

Many two- to four-unit purchases in Philadelphia come with tenants in place. That is often fine, because occupied units keep rent coming in while the vacant one is renovated. It does require planning.

We phase work so the occupied units keep heat, water and safe access throughout the job. Shared systems such as the main service, the boiler or the roof are scheduled with advance notice to tenants, and shutdowns are kept short. Lead-safe practices are especially important in occupied buildings, since dust can migrate through stairwells and shared basements. When a vacant unit is complete and leased, we move to the next as it turns over. Your field manager keeps the schedule, posts progress and tracks each unit's scope separately so the draw record matches the work done in each apartment. On narrow Philadelphia streets, we also coordinate deliveries and dumpster placement so tenants and neighbors are not blocked in.

faqs.q: What types of small multifamily buildings do you renovate in Philadelphia?
faqs.a: We work on stacked duplexes in the Northeast, converted twins in West Philadelphia and Germantown, larger rowhouses in North Philadelphia that hold two or three units, and small four-unit buildings across the city. Each type comes with its own common issues, from shared boilers to missing fire separation, and our scopes are written around the specific building rather than a template.

faqs.q: Can you add a unit to a Philadelphia rowhouse?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Adding a unit generally requires a zoning permit from Licenses and Inspections and may need a variance from the Zoning Board of Adjustment, depending on the zoning district. If it is allowed, the work includes fire separation, egress, separate utilities and a kitchen and bath. We can estimate the construction cost so you can weigh it against the time and uncertainty of the approval process.

faqs.q: Can tenants stay during the renovation?
faqs.a: Often, yes. We phase work so occupied units keep heat, water and safe access, give notice before shared-system shutdowns and follow lead-safe practices to keep dust out of occupied spaces. Some scopes, such as replacing a shared roof or main service, may require brief interruptions. Your field manager plans those in advance and keeps you updated on each unit, so you can communicate clearly with your tenants and property manager.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Philadelphia, PA | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) certified contractor for Philadelphia buyers, agents and lenders: rowhouse bids, Limited vs Standard scopes, consultant reports and draw schedules.
fha-203k.intro: Plenty of Philadelphia rowhouses are priced within reach of first-time buyers precisely because they need work: a tired roof, a kitchen from another era, wiring nobody wants to inspect. An FHA 203(k) loan lets a buyer finance the purchase and the repairs together, and Genstone Construction is an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor that prepares the bids, scopes and draw schedules lenders need. We work with buyers, real estate agents and loan officers across Philadelphia, from porch-front rowhouses in Olney and Mayfair to brick twins in Germantown and Mount Airy. Our estimators write a scope that matches the loan type, a designated field manager coordinates vetted local contractors and permits through Licenses and Inspections, and draws follow the lender's process so the buyer is never asked to pay upfront.

sections.h2: Limited or Standard: which fits a Philadelphia rowhouse
sections.body:
The Limited 203(k) covers non-structural repairs up to $75,000 and suits many Philadelphia porch-front and post-war rowhouses. A typical Limited scope might include a new roof, replacement windows, an updated kitchen and bath, a new water heater or boiler, electrical panel replacement, and flooring and paint. It does not allow structural work, so a house with a bowed rear wall or failing joists is not a Limited candidate.

The Standard 203(k) is built for heavier projects and requires a minimum of $5,000 in repairs and a HUD-approved 203(k) consultant. In Philadelphia, that usually means older rowhouses with masonry repairs, structural framing, rear wall rebuilding, or layout changes like adding a second-floor bath. Standard loans take longer to close because the consultant prepares the work write-up and the lender reviews it, but they let a buyer take on a house that the Limited program would not cover. Our estimators help agents and buyers see quickly which program the house points toward.

sections.h2: Philadelphia houses that tend to work well with 203(k)
sections.body:
The strongest 203(k) candidates here are houses that are structurally sound but cosmetically and mechanically dated. Porch-front rowhouses in Olney, Logan, Oxford Circle and Kingsessing often fit that description: solid brick, decent layouts and original kitchens, baths and wiring. Post-war rowhomes in Mayfair and Rhawnhurst are similar, with garages and basements that buyers like once the systems are modernized.

Older 19th-century rowhouses can work too, but they deserve a careful inspection first. Masonry, joist pockets, sewer laterals and roof framing in those houses are more likely to push the project into Standard territory. Because nearly all Philadelphia rowhouses were built before 1978, FHA lead-based paint requirements apply when painted surfaces are disturbed, and our scope accounts for lead-safe work and clearance where required. Agents find it helpful to send us a listing early, so we can flag likely structural issues before the buyer writes an offer and the appraisal is ordered.

sections.h2: Bids, consultants and draws on a Philadelphia 203(k)
sections.body:
Lenders need a detailed contractor bid that lines up with the 203(k) consultant's work write-up on Standard loans or with the lender's requirements on Limited loans. We itemize each repair with labor and materials, list the permits Licenses and Inspections will require and propose a draw schedule tied to completed milestones.

During construction, a designated field manager coordinates vetted local contractors and keeps the lender, buyer and consultant informed. Draw requests follow the lender's inspection and approval process, and repairs over the $15,000 threshold may involve additional inspections before funds are released. Lien waivers are collected with each draw. Because the buyer often needs to move in on a schedule, we sequence the work so the most essential systems, such as roof, heat and electrical, are finished early. When the job is complete, the buyer receives final documentation and our one-year workmanship warranty, which covers our work but not normal wear or damage after move-in.

faqs.q: Is Genstone an approved FHA 203(k) contractor?
faqs.a: Yes. We hold FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor status and prepare detailed bids and scopes that fit Limited and Standard 203(k) loans, coordinate with HUD consultants on Standard loans, and follow lender draw procedures. In Philadelphia, we coordinate vetted, licensed local contractors, with a designated field manager overseeing the project and handling permits with Licenses and Inspections. Buyers and agents get one point of contact from bid through final draw.

faqs.q: Can a Limited 203(k) cover a new roof on a Philadelphia rowhouse?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. Replacing a flat roof membrane and flashing is generally treated as a non-structural repair and can fit within a Limited 203(k), as long as total repairs stay under $75,000 and the roof deck framing is sound. If rafters or joists need replacement, the project may need the Standard program instead. We confirm that during the bid so there are no surprises later.

faqs.q: How early should an agent involve you in a 203(k) purchase?
faqs.a: As early as possible. Ideally, we see the listing or inspection report before the buyer makes an offer so we can flag structural issues, estimate repairs and suggest whether a Limited or Standard loan fits. Getting a bid to the lender quickly helps keep the closing on track. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review is available to agents and buyers as well as investors.

reo-renovation.title: REO Property Renovation in Philadelphia, PA | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: Bank-owned and servicer REO renovation in Philadelphia: vacant property license, doors and windows rules, freeze damage, L&I violations and documented repairs.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Renovations in Philadelphia
reo-renovation.intro: Vacant rowhouses in Philadelphia deteriorate in predictable ways. Boilers freeze and split, roofs leak into back bedrooms, copper pipe disappears, and the house collects Licenses and Inspections violations that follow it into the REO file. Genstone Construction works with mortgage servicers, banks, investment funds and other lenders, and is a preferred contractor for Government-Sponsored Enterprises. We coordinate vetted, licensed local contractors in Philadelphia to secure, repair and prepare bank-owned properties for sale or rent, with a designated field manager responsible for each asset. Scopes are built around the city's vacant-property rules and the specific damage found on site, and every step is documented with photos and line-item estimates so asset managers can approve work and report on it without traveling to the property. Genstone Field Services also provides preservation, inspections and code compliance work.

sections.h2: Philadelphia's vacant-property rules and what they mean for servicers
sections.body:
Owners of vacant buildings in Philadelphia generally need a vacant property license from Licenses and Inspections, and the city expects vacant structures to be secured and maintained. The doors and windows ordinance requires working doors and windows, rather than boarded openings, on vacant buildings in blocks where most houses are occupied. When an owner does not act, the city can clean and seal the property and bill the cost.

For servicers and banks, that means REO work in Philadelphia often starts with compliance. We review open violations, confirm license status and scope the work needed to clear them, such as replacing boarded openings with windows and doors, removing debris, repairing hazardous steps or railings and correcting exterior defects. Clearing violations early lowers the risk of fines and makes the property easier to market. Our documentation, including before and after photos, helps your team respond to city notices and keep a clean record on the asset.

sections.h2: Freeze damage, water and vandalism in vacant rowhouses
sections.body:
Many Philadelphia rowhouses heat with hot-water boilers and cast-iron radiators. When a house sits vacant through a winter without proper winterization, water in the system freezes, cracks radiators and boiler sections and splits pipes. Thawing then floods floors and ceilings. We see this often in REO inventory, and it changes the scope from a cosmetic refresh to a mechanical and water-damage job.

Our REO scopes start with a careful inspection of the heating system, plumbing, roof and basement. Typical items include pressure testing supply lines, replacing frozen boilers or radiators, removing wet plaster and insulation, treating mold and drying framing before closing walls. Roof leaks are common in vacant houses because nobody notices them for months. Vandalism and copper theft can strip a house of plumbing, wiring and fixtures. We document each condition so your team can file claims, approve repairs and adjust the marketing plan with accurate information about the house as it stands.

sections.h2: Repair scopes that fit how the asset will be sold
sections.body:
Not every Philadelphia REO should get the same treatment. Some properties are best sold as-is to investors after securing, cleaning and clearing violations. Others will sell faster and for more after a targeted repair scope that makes them financeable, such as a working heat source, a sound roof, safe electrical and a functioning kitchen and bath. Some benefit from a full renovation, especially on blocks where renovated houses sell well.

Our estimators can write multiple scopes for the same asset, each with cost and projected value, so asset managers can choose the path that fits their disposition strategy. Every scope is line-itemized with labor, materials and debris removal included. A designated field manager coordinates local contractors, permits with Licenses and Inspections and inspections, and posts photos and milestone updates. Lien waivers and contractor compliance documents are collected, and draws or invoices follow your approval process. That documentation is often what servicers need most when they report to investors or GSE partners.

faqs.q: Do you handle clean-outs and securing before renovation?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone Field Services handles property preservation, including securing, debris removal, winterization and inspections, and Genstone Construction handles the renovation scope. In Philadelphia, securing must account for the doors and windows ordinance where it applies, which can mean installing working doors and windows rather than boarding. Debris and dumpster costs are included in our estimates, and every visit is logged with photos for your file.

faqs.q: Can you help clear Licenses and Inspections violations on an REO?
faqs.a: We can review open violations, scope the work needed to correct them, pull the necessary permits and schedule inspections. Common items include unsafe steps and railings, broken windows, roof defects, exterior masonry and debris. Our field manager documents completed corrections with photos so your team or legal counsel can follow up with the city on the case status and close out each violation on record.

faqs.q: Do you work with GSEs and institutional servicers?
faqs.a: Yes. Government-Sponsored Enterprises list Genstone as a preferred contractor, and our Philadelphia REO work is done for mortgage servicers, banks, REITs and investment funds. We provide line-item estimates, photo documentation, lien waivers and contractor compliance records, and we can adapt reporting to your platform or approval process. Projects in Philadelphia are coordinated through vetted, licensed local contractors, with a single field manager accountable for each asset.
